metadata.file_name: 5. Song & Cutumisu. (2024). Using machine learning to predict student science achievement based on science curriculum type in TIMSS 2019.pdf
metadata.title: Using machine learning to predict student science achievement based on science curriculum type in TIMSS 2019

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science microdata and extracts variables via IEA IDB Analyzer and SPSS, then merges and cleans the dataset before analysis. The analytic sample is restricted to 44 countries and to the Grade 8 Science assessment context, yielding 309,511 remaining entries after cleaning. For weighting, the authors explicitly use the science teacher weight (SCIWGT) because the key process-dimension variables (e.g., instructional clarity, instructional strategies, homework and experiment-related items) are reported by science teachers; they argue this reduces sampling bias for curriculum-to-achievement comparisons from an instructional perspective. The manuscript does not report applying student sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures for the ML prediction stage, so the weighting approach appears to focus on teacher-level weighting rather than full complex-survey student-weighted estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data; extracted variables of interest with IEA IDB Analyzer and merged in SPSS. After data cleaning, 309,511 entries from 44 countries remained. Curriculum type was defined using TIMSS ITCOURSE: students with ITCOURSE=6 were classified as integrated science; students with ITCOURSE in {2,3,4,5} were classified as separated science. The dependent variable was the science achievement plausible values (BSSSCI01–BSSSCI05), with separate analyses conducted for each PV.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Instructional strategy: link to prior knowledge

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (44 countries) — science achievement (BSSSCI01–BSSSCI05)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison using RMSE and R² on train/test splits (70%/30%) averaged across PVs. Random Forest: Testing R²=0.51, RMSE=74.92; Linear regression: Testing R²=0.21, RMSE=94.43; Lasso: Testing R²=0.22, RMSE=94.24; Decision tree: Testing R²=0.29, RMSE=89.88; Neural networks: Testing R²=0.22, RMSE=94.34. Feature importance (RF) indicates curriculum type has the smallest average coefficient (0.010) relative to SES (0.215) and confidence (0.094).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science the study leveraged socio-economic background, students’ confidence about science, instructional time, and science experiment frequency (with curriculum type as a covariate) to predict science achievement plausible values, finding that Random Forest outperformed linear regression, lasso, decision trees, and neural networks and that curriculum type was a weak direct predictor compared with SES and instructional/process variables. This indicates that curriculum structure may influence science literacy indirectly through instructional conditions and student attitudes, so policy should prioritize implementation quality (e.g., instructional time and experiment practices) rather than assuming integrated curricula automatically yield large achievement gains, though causality cannot be inferred from predictive feature importance alone.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (44 countries) — science achievement (Plausible Values BSSSCI01–BSSSCI05)
main_findings.target_variable: Curriculum effect on science achievement (Average Treatment Effect via propensity score matching)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Propensity score estimation via stacked ensemble (base learners: k-NN, Random Forest, Naive Bayes; meta-learner: logistic regression) with KNN matching. Propensity score prediction accuracy on test set: 0.9998. After matching, Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction show integrated curricula have significantly higher science achievement than separated curricula for each PV (Cohen’s d around 0.2; e.g., PV1 d=0.22 with integrated mean 546.62 vs separated mean 515.68; PV2 d=0.20; PV3 d=0.24; PV4 d=0.23; PV5 d=0.20).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science the study leveraged propensity score matching based on socio-economic background, student attitudes, and instructional clarity to estimate the average treatment effect of integrated versus separated science curricula on science achievement plausible values, finding that integrated curricula produced a statistically significant but small advantage (Cohen’s d ≈0.2 across PVs). This indicates that integrated curricula may be beneficial in practice, but the magnitude is modest, so education systems should treat curriculum integration as one component within a broader package that ensures instructional prerequisites and high-quality implementation, while recognizing that matching on observed covariates cannot fully eliminate unobserved confounding.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data from 44 countries, classifying students as integrated or separated science using TIMSS ITCOURSE (ITCOURSE=6 vs 2/3/4/5). For the curriculum effect, it estimates propensity scores using a stacked ensemble (k-NN, Random Forest, Naive Bayes as base learners; logistic regression as meta-learner) and matches integrated to separated students using KNN; after matching, Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction show integrated curricula have significantly higher science achievement across all five plausible values, with small effect sizes (Cohen’s d around 0.2). For prediction, it compares linear regression, lasso, decision trees, Random Forest, and neural networks using RMSE and R² on a 70/30 train/test split averaged across PVs; Random Forest performs best (testing R²=0.51, RMSE=74.92). Feature importance indicates socio-economic background, confidence, instructional time, and experiment frequency dominate, while curriculum type has a small coefficient. Limitations include reliance on predictive associations (not causal identification) and limited reporting of full complex-survey weighting beyond teacher weights.
